capabilities.target: Postgres database via service-role execute_sql, bypassing row level security; includes an integration_tokens table
support_messages table rows, rendered back to the customer in the support UI

inputs.source: Developer's direct prompt in the IDE chat ('Show me the latest open support tickets')
Customer-submitted ticket message via the public support widget, later retrieved into agent context when tickets are read

elements.name: Supabase/Postgres database (includes integration_tokens and support_messages tables)
Customer using the public support widget
Customer ticket message ingress into the database
Agent write of reply/query content into support_messages, rendered to the customer
Developer prompt entering the agent within the IDE session

controls.name: IDE client per-call tool invocation approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The IDE shows the raw SQL for each call and requires developer approval before execution, enforced by the client outside the model; this does not weaken as model capability grows, but its practical effectiveness depends on approval volume (approval fatigue), not model capability.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting database role for ticket-driven queries
controls.decay_rationale: A properly scoped credential does not decay with model capability; restricting the role's access excludes sensitive tables such as integration_tokens regardless of what the model is instructed to do.

controls.name: Outbound DLP filter on writes to customer-visible tables
controls.decay_rationale: A pattern-based filter enforced outside the model can catch obvious secret formats, but encoded or paraphrased secrets can get past it as the model becomes more capable at evading pattern matches; it narrows rather than severs the path.

controls.name: Pin and hash the Supabase MCP server package version
controls.decay_rationale: Version pinning and hash verification enforced at install time do not depend on model behavior; they prevent a silently updated or poisoned server package from being loaded regardless of what the model does.

controls.name: Row/size/rate limit on execute_sql calls
controls.decay_rationale: A hard limit enforced at the database or proxy layer does not depend on model behavior; it narrows the blast radius of any single approved call but does not make the sink unreachable.

controls.name: Append-only audit log of executed SQL and approving developer
controls.decay_rationale: An append-only log enforced outside the model does not decay with model capability; it earns no tier credit (detective only) but supports accountability if reviewed.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta via service-role confused deputy (TC1 + TC4): injected ticket content can drive a service-role read of integration tokens and an exfiltrating write back to the customer

attack_path.note: Customer submits a ticket containing attacker-crafted text, potentially including instructions aimed at the agent.
A benign developer request causes execute_sql to run with the service role, returning ticket content into context and able to reach other tables such as integration_tokens, bypassing RLS.
Agent inserts a reply (potentially containing exfiltrated data) into support_messages, which is rendered back to the customer, completing exfiltration to the attacker.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: IDE config changes to auto-approve or batch-approve tool calls, the approval gate disabled or bypassed, or autonomy raised beyond per-step approval.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database.
Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget, and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, creating an attacker-readable egress channel.
The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL, but developers approve many calls in a session, indicating high approval volume and fatigue risk.
The developer's innocuous request 'Show me the latest open support tickets' causes the agent to read ticket content using the service-role execute_sql capability.

recommendations.action: Use a row-level-security-respecting, least-privilege database role for any query path that can be influenced by customer-submitted content (ticket reads and replies); reserve the service-role key for explicit, developer-only administrative actions outside this path.
Add an outbound data-loss-prevention check before writing query results into customer-visible support_messages rows, blocking secret-like patterns such as tokens and keys.
Add a row/size/rate limit on execute_sql reads and writes to bound the blast radius of any single approved call.
Log every executed SQL statement together with the approving developer identity in an append-only audit store separate from the IDE session.
Tag ticket message content retrieved from the database as untrusted data in the agent's context (spotlighting) so the model is less likely to treat embedded text as instructions.

findings.title: Unpinned Supabase MCP server install ('@latest') leaves tool definitions and credentials open to a rug pull

threat_refs.name: Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: AI Agent Tools

forecast.watch_signal: The Supabase MCP server package publishes a new version under the same @latest tag, or a similarly named package appears, and npx fetches a different artifact than previously used without any version change being reviewed.

evidence.observation: The Supabase MCP server is invoked via 'npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest', using the @latest tag with no version pin or hash verification.
The server is granted an access token (${SUPABASE_PAT}) used for all database operations, so a poisoned server version would gain that credential.

recommendations.action: Pin the Supabase MCP server package to a specific version and verify its hash before each session instead of using the @latest tag.
Monitor for unexpected changes in the installed MCP server's tool list or schemas between sessions.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent runs as a single developer-invoked IDE process per session; there is no separate caller identity within this design that could be spoofed.
Artifacts do not describe any audit log of executed SQL tool calls distinct from the per-call IDE approval prompts.
Artifacts do not state a step, row, or spend limit for execute_sql calls beyond requiring developer approval per call.
Artifacts do not describe logging of the MCP server process's own actions separate from agent tool calls.
Artifacts do not state any rate limiting enforced by or on the MCP server process.
Artifacts do not describe query timeouts, connection limits, or storage quotas for the database.
Artifacts do not describe how customers are authenticated on the public support widget, so it is unclear whether a submitter's identity can be forged.
Artifacts do not describe whether ticket submissions are attributable to a verified customer account or session.
This inbound flow carries customer-authored text into the database; it does not itself move data out of the trust boundary, so outward disclosure does not apply to the ingress direction.
Artifacts do not describe rate limiting on ticket submissions through the public support widget.
Artifacts do not describe a limit on the volume or size of data written back into support_messages per call.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk reaches critical because an untrusted, customer-authored ticket message can reach a service-role database read that bypasses row-level security (including a table of integration tokens) and a customer-visible write capability, forming a complete lethal-trifecta attack path (TC1) compounded by a confused-deputy privilege issue (TC4). The only control in place, a per-call IDE approval prompt, is structural and shows raw SQL (independent of model capability) but is undermined by high approval volume (approval fatigue, ASI09 / SAFE-T1403), holding residual at high rather than lower. A second, independent finding notes that the Supabase MCP server is pulled unpinned via '@latest', a present supply-chain gap (ASI04) that could let a poisoned server bypass the approval gate entirely if exploited; it is capped at high as a property finding. Both findings forecast to critical if the approval gate is weakened further (autonomy increase or removal) or if a malicious server version is published, since neither trigger leaves any effective control in place. The single highest-leverage fix is replacing the service-role credential with a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role for ticket-driven queries.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt or agent instructions were provided; the agent's goal-handling behavior is inferred only from the runtime notes, which lowers confidence on instruction-related findings.

Exact table schema is not provided beyond naming support_messages and an integration tokens table; the 'restricted' sensitivity assigned to integration tokens is inferred from its description as credential data.
No logging or audit configuration is described; repudiation and denial-of-service properties are marked not_assessed rather than findings because the artifacts do not state whether they exist.
